Owners of Wang Fu Estate began choosing flats last week. Secretary for Housing Winnie Ho previously said 90.6% of owners have signed the Sale Agreement, reminding them to finalise signing before October 15. A legislator asked, with 10 days remaining until the 15th, how would the authority handle outstanding sale agreements? Ho said if owners are "in good faith," the authority would certainly show understanding and make flexible arrangements as far as possible. She also said that if owners "have no intention to negotiate," they would be deemed as no longer accepting the acquisition scheme, and legislation in the future could not be ruled out. As for some owners having to pay stamp duty amounting to six figures, Ho said the government's acquisition price is 30% higher than market value, with relevant factors already taken into account, describing "that 30% is precisely where reason and law meet emotion."

Secretary for Housing Winnie Ho recently said 90.6% of owners have signed the sale agreement. A legislator asked, with 99.3% of owners accepting the acquisition and 10 days remaining until October 15, how would the authority assess the progress? (File photo)

Secretary for Housing Winnie Ho attended a policy briefing at the Legislative Council today (the 5th). DAB legislator Tang Ka-piu said that, as Wang Fu Estate owners have recently been choosing flats, many have praised the explainers as "doing a great job," being well-versed in procedures and policies, and showing empathy towards residents' needs. He said they deserve commendation and praised the team's hard work.

Ho said on a radio programme on Saturday (the 3rd) that 90.6% of Wang Fu Estate owners have completed signing the Sale Agreement, and reminded owners to complete signing by October 15. Tang Ka-piu asked, with 99.3% of owners accepting the acquisition and resettlement and only 10 days remaining, how would the authority handle owners who have not signed by October 15? He revealed that a case he is following involves a family who wishes to accept the acquisition, but the original owner has passed away and court proceedings are underway, describing them as "very anxious." He asked whether they could retain the right to choose a flat if they cannot complete the process on time.

Ho (right) said if owners are "in good faith" about completing the transaction, the authority will show understanding and make flexible arrangements. As for owners who "have no intention to negotiate," legislation in the future could not be ruled out. (File photo)

Ho says flexible arrangements will be made if owners are "in good faith"

Ho said the question is not directly related to the five-year plan and gave a brief response. She first praised the explanation team, saying "the explanation team is in fact best able to help residents," because each of the more than 1,980 households has different circumstances and intentions. She said the team "truly accompanies each household forward," understanding their difficulties or what they require to make a decision, and hoped everyone would communicate more with the explainers.

She continued that October 15 is an important date, and said two situations may arise where the agreement cannot be completed by then. The first is when owners very much wish to complete the transaction but are unable due to circumstances beyond their control, such as sudden illness and hospitalisation preventing them from signing documents. She said as long as it is clear that owners are acting in good faith to conclude the transaction and the reasons are beyond their control, "we will certainly show understanding and make flexible arrangements as far as possible." The other situation is when "they begin to have no intention to negotiate," or refuse to sign documents, fail to handle procedures, and show "no such intention." In such cases, "we have to regard them as no longer accepting this acquisition scheme, and our sale will be terminated." Ho said it cannot be ruled out that this group of people will be like the dozen or so households who initially did not return the acceptance letters, and the government has said on multiple occasions that legislation may be required in the future.

Many Wang Fu Estate owners expressed that they were forced to change flats yet had to pay hefty stamp duty. Ho responded to legislators by saying that when the government proposed an acquisition price 30% higher than market value, it had already taken relevant factors into account. (File photo)

Responding to questions about hefty stamp duty, Ho says "acquisition price is 30% higher"

Tang Ka-piu further asked that some owners choosing more expensive projects in Kowloon Bay and Fanling have to pay six-figure stamp duty, and asked "is there anything that can alleviate this immediate financial burden?" He also mentioned that about 20 households in Wang Chi House have purchased home insurance, pointing out that residents of the other seven blocks received insurance compensation after the fire due to the insurance companies' consideration, but Wang Chi House has not received similar help, and "hoped the government would also help residents of Wang Chi House."

Ho did not respond to questions about insurance for Wang Chi House. Addressing stamp duty, Ho said the acquisition price is 30% higher than market value, and "that 30% is precisely where reason and law meet emotion." She said she had previously explained in the Legislative Council that "this 30% recognises that they may need to relocate, have some renovation costs, legal fees, or stamp duty on property transactions. If the 30% has already taken these situations into account, then stamp duty is also covered within these considerations." She added that the rent allowance would be extended until residents purchase their new units, and Tung Wah Group of Hospitals also provides pro bono legal assistance.

Ho also pointed out that in fact many units are priced below HK$4 million, and for nearly two-thirds of the units, the acquisition price without land premium supplement is sufficient for owners to make a purchase. Owners choosing such units only need to pay HK$100 in stamp duty. She said all of this shows that while balancing public resources, the authority is doing its utmost to help residents, so that they can find a place to settle as soon as possible.
